Frequently Asked Questions
Prop 42 is a measure on the November 3, 2026 ballot (https://urldefense.proofpoint.com/v2/url?u=https-3A__vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov_2026_general_pdf_prop42-2Dtext-2Dproposed-2Dlaws.pdf&d=DwMGaQ&c=euGZstcaTDllvimEN8b7jXrwqOf-v5A_CdpgnVfiiMM&r=Lbak5eFZHnZSYhftzpqbORUrs1mHGbmgfEVBYVeetqU&m=3Kh86csSe4Cl6q9fcUvr1QX3IGpDHhcugmEJous0LV6L-5TYZP1t6L6mee4OHIHn&s=c3Gqu-OMIDatgK3hnMmB3S2ODmqsGQ0poGtXleReCu8&e=) that protects Californians from double taxation on the money we earn by closing a loophole (https://urldefense.proofpoint.com/v2/url?u=https-3A__voterguide.sos.ca.gov_propositions_42_&d=DwMGaQ&c=euGZstcaTDllvimEN8b7jXrwqOf-v5A_CdpgnVfiiMM&r=Lbak5eFZHnZSYhftzpqbORUrs1mHGbmgfEVBYVeetqU&m=3Kh86csSe4Cl6q9fcUvr1QX3IGpDHhcugmEJous0LV6L-5TYZP1t6L6mee4OHIHn&s=ufUF2OJehlbx--9fM7nvGFw4Qh_D0Cgtj_UKws5-HY0&e=) in California’s Constitution that allows new state taxes on retirement accounts, personal savings, pensions, and other personal property.
Updated October 13, 2026
What is Prop 42 (2026)? (javascript:void(0))
Prop 42, the Retirement & Personal Savings Protection Act of 2026, protects Californians from double taxation on the money we earn (https://urldefense.proofpoint.com/v2/url?u=https-3A__voterguide.sos.ca.gov_propositions_42_&d=DwMGaQ&c=euGZstcaTDllvimEN8b7jXrwqOf-v5A_CdpgnVfiiMM&r=Lbak5eFZHnZSYhftzpqbORUrs1mHGbmgfEVBYVeetqU&m=3Kh86csSe4Cl6q9fcUvr1QX3IGpDHhcugmEJous0LV6L-5TYZP1t6L6mee4OHIHn&s=ufUF2OJehlbx--9fM7nvGFw4Qh_D0Cgtj_UKws5-HY0&e=) by closing a loophole in California’s Constitution that allows new state taxes on retirement accounts, personal savings, pensions, and other personal property.
You already pay income taxes when you earn your money. Proposition 42 (2026) ensures the state cannot tax that same money twice simply because it is sitting in a retirement account or savings account. It also prohibits retroactive taxes (https://urldefense.proofpoint.com/v2/url?u=https-3A__vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov_2026_general_pdf_prop42-2Dtext-2Dproposed-2Dlaws.pdf&d=DwMGaQ&c=euGZstcaTDllvimEN8b7jXrwqOf-v5A_CdpgnVfiiMM&r=Lbak5eFZHnZSYhftzpqbORUrs1mHGbmgfEVBYVeetqU&m=3Kh86csSe4Cl6q9fcUvr1QX3IGpDHhcugmEJous0LV6L-5TYZP1t6L6mee4OHIHn&s=c3Gqu-OMIDatgK3hnMmB3S2ODmqsGQ0poGtXleReCu8&e=) that would change the rules after you’ve already earned and saved.
You earned and saved it. Prop 42 (2026) protects it.
Why is Prop 42 Needed? (javascript:void(0))
California is the third most expensive state (https://urldefense.proofpoint.com/v2/url?u=https-3A__www.cnbc.com_make-2Dit_2025_01_19_most-2Dexpensive-2Dus-2Dstates-2Dto-2Dretire.html&d=DwMGaQ&c=euGZstcaTDllvimEN8b7jXrwqOf-v5A_CdpgnVfiiMM&r=Lbak5eFZHnZSYhftzpqbORUrs1mHGbmgfEVBYVeetqU&m=3Kh86csSe4Cl6q9fcUvr1QX3IGpDHhcugmEJous0LV6L-5TYZP1t6L6mee4OHIHn&s=q3QbdWzqFeD9B_wUx9JL86V-tLjHuGtDqGwUv2vctdw&e=) for retirees. Our high cost of living and high taxes already make it difficult for people to get ahead or to save enough for retirement. A recent survey of Californians found that 73% know someone who has had to delay retirement for financial reasons.
Californians deserve peace of mind that their hard-earned savings will be there when they need them. Yet, California’s Constitution allows the Legislature and special interests to impose new state taxes on retirement accounts and personal savings. It should be illegal for politicians and special interests to tax our retirement and savings. Prop 42 (2026) closes that loophole (https://urldefense.proofpoint.com/v2/url?u=https-3A__vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov_2026_general_pdf_prop42-2Dtext-2Dproposed-2Dlaws.pdf&d=DwMGaQ&c=euGZstcaTDllvimEN8b7jXrwqOf-v5A_CdpgnVfiiMM&r=Lbak5eFZHnZSYhftzpqbORUrs1mHGbmgfEVBYVeetqU&m=3Kh86csSe4Cl6q9fcUvr1QX3IGpDHhcugmEJous0LV6L-5TYZP1t6L6mee4OHIHn&s=c3Gqu-OMIDatgK3hnMmB3S2ODmqsGQ0poGtXleReCu8&e=) and protects retirement, life savings and personal property from new taxes.
Can the Legislature Pass Taxes on Retirement & Life Savings Today? (javascript:void(0))
Yes. California's Constitution currently gives the Legislature the authority to impose taxes on personal property such as retirement accounts, pensions, 401(k)s, IRAs, bank accounts, and other personal savings.
In recent years, lawmakers have introduced five separate bills proposing taxes on retirement savings and other personal property. Although none became law, these attempts underscore that this authority already exists and has been tried repeatedly.
The Legislature should not be able to tax retirement accounts. Prop 42 (2026) provides that protection by closing the loophole in California's Constitution before it can be used to tax retirement savings and personal property.
What Does Prop 42 Protect? (javascript:void(0))
Prop 42 (2026) (https://urldefense.proofpoint.com/v2/url?u=https-3A__voterguide.sos.ca.gov_propositions_42_&d=DwMGaQ&c=euGZstcaTDllvimEN8b7jXrwqOf-v5A_CdpgnVfiiMM&r=Lbak5eFZHnZSYhftzpqbORUrs1mHGbmgfEVBYVeetqU&m=3Kh86csSe4Cl6q9fcUvr1QX3IGpDHhcugmEJous0LV6L-5TYZP1t6L6mee4OHIHn&s=ufUF2OJehlbx--9fM7nvGFw4Qh_D0Cgtj_UKws5-HY0&e=) protects retirement accounts, including 401(k)s, pensions, IRAs, and other retirement plans. It also protects personal savings accounts and other personal property that could otherwise be subject to new state taxes.
How Would a Tax on Retirement Savings Affect My 401(k)? (javascript:void(0))
Even a small annual tax on retirement savings could reduce both the value of your retirement savings and the investment growth that helps build retirement security over time.
A recent economic analysis (https://urldefense.proofpoint.com/v2/url?u=https-3A__www.morningstar.com_news_pr-2Dnewswire_20260929la57497_10000-2Da-2Dyear-2Dtax-2Don-2Dretirement-2Dnew-2Dreport-2Dshows-2Dhow-2Deven-2Da-2Dsmall-2Dtax-2Don-2Dyour-2Dretirement-2Dcan-2Dhave-2Dhuge-2Dimpact-2Don-2Dyour-2Dfinances&d=DwMGaQ&c=euGZstcaTDllvimEN8b7jXrwqOf-v5A_CdpgnVfiiMM&r=Lbak5eFZHnZSYhftzpqbORUrs1mHGbmgfEVBYVeetqU&m=3Kh86csSe4Cl6q9fcUvr1QX3IGpDHhcugmEJous0LV6L-5TYZP1t6L6mee4OHIHn&s=ZTMu5TxB_roUrtTd3dWzB9ulnZEAslHk2U4ENj0Fggc&e=) found that even a 1% tax on retirement could cause middle-class Californians to face annual tax bills of up to $10,000 and have to work up to seven additional years before retiring. Prop 42 (2026) protects 401(k)s and other retirement savings from new state taxes that would chip into retirement savings or force Californians to delay retirement.
Does Prop 42 Impact Existing Programs or Funding? (javascript:void(0))
No. Prop 42 (2026) does not reduce existing funding for schools, public safety, healthcare, transportation, or other state programs. It simply prohibits new state taxes on retirement savings and other personal property. Existing revenue sources and funding formulas remain unchanged.
Does Prop 42 Only Protect Wealthy Californians? (javascript:void(0))
No. Prop 42 (2026) protects everyone who works and saves for retirement, including teachers, firefighters, police officers, veterans, retirees, small business owners, and middle-class families. If you have retirement savings or personal savings, Prop 42 (2026) protects you.
Who Supports Prop 42? (javascript:void(0))
Prop 42 (2026) is supported by a broad coalition of seniors, firefighters, veterans, building trades workers, small businesses, and working families who believe Californians should not pay taxes twice on the money they earn and save. This includes the California Professional Firefighters, California Senior Alliance, AMVETS, Dept. of California, State Building and Construction Trades Council of California, Peace Officers Research Association of California, and the California Small Business Association.

By The Editorial Board (https://www.sandiegouniontribune.com/author/the-editorial-board/) | opinion@scng.com (mailto:opinion@scng.com)
PUBLISHED: September 21, 2026 at 2:39 PM PDT | UPDATED: September 21, 2026 at 2:56 PM PDT
Getting your Trinity Audio (https://trinityaudio.ai/) player ready...
The most hotly debated initiative on the November ballot is Proposition 40, which would impose a 5% tax on the wealth of California billionaires. As this Editorial Board opined (https://www.ocregister.com/2026/09/13/endorsement-no-on-proposition-40s-reckless-wealth-tax/) in our opposition, the union-created Billionaire Tax Act would send a dangerous message to current and future entrepreneurs, and “have a chilling effect on investment.”
But two closely related measures, Propositions 41 and 42 (https://www.bakersfield.com/opinion/our-view/our-view-vote-no-on-propositions-40-41-42-tax-propositions-hurt-state-californians/article_1c8492b8-5fb9-4897-9f1c-c9ba56460e0d.amp.html) , have received much less attention — partly because they’re so complicated. By adding related measures to the ballot, opponents of Prop. 40 are hoping that voters approve one of these alternatives that will derail Prop. 40. Because these two measures have elements that contradict Prop. 40, the one that gets the highest vote totals (if voters OK them all) would go into effect.
Adding similar-sounding measures also muddies the waters, thus increasing the likelihood that confused voters vote “no” on all of them — thus accomplishing the main goal of stopping the billionaires’ tax. But our goal isn’t to map out political strategies (https://www.pbs.org/wgbh/americanexperience/features/nash-game/) . It’s a worthy effort to try to stop a disastrous new tax scheme.
Besides their intended purpose of blocking Prop. 40, the measures could protect taxpayers for years to come.
Specifically, Prop. 41 would require one-time audits of programs that any proposed special taxes would fund. Those audits, which must be completed before the initiative appears on the ballot, would be required to identify ways that such programs could cut annual costs by 10%, per an analysis (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=41&year=2026) from the Legislative Analyst’s Office.
While Prop. 40 exempts itself from state spending limits, Prop. 41 also requires new special-tax revenues to count toward the Gann Limit (https://www.sheehystrategygroup.com/news/2026/3/9/californias-state-appropriations-limit-gann-limit) — the 1979 constitutional amendment that caps the revenue the state can spend each year. The state has passed a number of workarounds over the years, but applying new revenues to this formula would potentially require the return of certain additional tax revenues to taxpayers (https://www.yesonprop41.org/about-prop41) and the earmarking of revenues to infrastructure.
Prop. 42 is more straightforward. Per theLAO (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=42&year=2026), the initiative prohibits “new taxes on the ownership of financial assets or other personal property.” California doesn’t currently tax the ownership of financial assets and only taxes personal property in a limited way (e.g., vehicle license fees), but the measure’s passage “could make it somewhat harder for the state to raise taxes.” It also limits imposition of retroactive taxes.
So would the Editorial Board support these measures even if they were standalone initiatives? The answers are unequivocal: Yes and yes.

The most hotly debated initiative on the November ballot is Proposition 40, which would impose a 5% tax on the wealth of California billionaires. As this Editorial Board opined (https://www.ocregister.com/2026/09/13/endorsement-no-on-proposition-40s-reckless-wealth-tax/) in our opposition, the union-created Billionaire Tax Act would send a dangerous message to current and future entrepreneurs, and “have a chilling effect on investment.”
But two closely related measures, Propositions 41 and 42 (https://www.bakersfield.com/opinion/our-view/our-view-vote-no-on-propositions-40-41-42-tax-propositions-hurt-state-californians/article_1c8492b8-5fb9-4897-9f1c-c9ba56460e0d.amp.html) , have received much less attention — partly because they’re so complicated. By adding related measures to the ballot, opponents of Prop. 40 are hoping that voters approve one of these alternatives that will derail Prop. 40. Because these two measures have elements that contradict Prop. 40, the one that gets the highest vote totals (if voters OK them all) would go into effect.
Adding similar-sounding measures also muddies the waters, thus increasing the likelihood that confused voters vote “no” on all of them — thus accomplishing the main goal of stopping the billionaires’ tax. But our goal isn’t to map out political strategies (https://www.pbs.org/wgbh/americanexperience/features/nash-game/) . It’s a worthy effort to try to stop a disastrous new tax scheme.
Besides their intended purpose of blocking Prop. 40, the measures could protect taxpayers for years to come.
Specifically, Prop. 41 would require one-time audits of programs that any proposed special taxes would fund. Those audits, which must be completed before the initiative appears on the ballot, would be required to identify ways that such programs could cut annual costs by 10%, per an analysis (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=41&year=2026) from the Legislative Analyst’s Office.
While Prop. 40 exempts itself from state spending limits, Prop. 41 also requires new special-tax revenues to count toward the Gann Limit (https://www.sheehystrategygroup.com/news/2026/3/9/californias-state-appropriations-limit-gann-limit) — the 1979 constitutional amendment that caps the revenue the state can spend each year. The state has passed a number of workarounds over the years, but applying new revenues to this formula would potentially require the return of certain additional tax revenues to taxpayers (https://www.yesonprop41.org/about-prop41) and the earmarking of revenues to infrastructure.
Prop. 42 is more straightforward. Per theLAO (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=42&year=2026), the initiative prohibits “new taxes on the ownership of financial assets or other personal property.” California doesn’t currently tax the ownership of financial assets and only taxes personal property in a limited way (e.g., vehicle license fees), but the measure’s passage “could make it somewhat harder for the state to raise taxes.” It also limits imposition of retroactive taxes.
So would the Editorial Board support these measures even if they were standalone initiatives? The answers are unequivocal: Yes and yes.

Successive waves of federal cuts to California’s safety net are hitting our shores — and hospitals.
H.R. 1 (aka the “One Big Beautiful Bill Act”), the spending plan written by House Republicans and signed into law last year by President Donald Trump, included the largest reductions in U.S. history to food assistance and health care programs. Its intentionally punitive and retaliatory cuts to California’s Medicaid program, Medi-Cal, are projected to cost the state billions of dollars per year and lead to more than a million Californians losing access to health care.
In the Bay Area, these cuts are becoming painful.
As our news organization documented this month, the number of uninsured people in emergency rooms at Santa Clara Valley Healthcare and Alameda Health System has spiked year over year.

Those county-run systems expect to collectively lose more than a billion dollars annually. Notably, while our systems and residents are scrambling to survive, rural America is receiving a $50 billion lifeline from House Republicans and President Trump to protect their health care systems.
Proposition 40 was written to prop up this state’s safety net in the face of these devastating cuts.
However, this measure is the wrong solution to a real problem.
We advise California voters to reject short-sighted, self-sabotaging Proposition 40.
And we recommend they reject equally myopic Propositions 41 and 42 — countermeasures that would not only nullify the billionaires tax but senselessly shackle the state’s fiscal future.
Killing Golden Goose
Proposition 40 risks long-term pain for short-term gain. It’s the ballot equivalent of eating your seed corn.
Here’s how it would work:
Proposition 40 would impose a one-time 5% levy on the net worth of billionaires who were residents of California on January 1. The tax would be due next year, but the state’s 250 or so billionaires could spread the payments out over five years.
Ninety percent of the revenues raised — estimated anywhere between $40 billion to $100 billion, depending on the expert — would fund health care services. The rest would go toward education and food assistance and administration.
What distinguishes this tax isn’t just that it’s targeting a very base of extremely high-net worth individuals but also that it applies retroactively and taxes wealth, not income.
Wealth taxes are unpopular with many economists, including liberal ones, for several reasons:
They can force the sale of productive assets (e.g. stock shares, patents, copyrights, farmland, etc). They’re difficult to administer because determining the value of some intangible assets, unlike income, is more art than a science. And most injuriously, they can encourage capital flight, especially when executed by a state acting alone.
To be sure, the capital hasn’t fled California yet, but the capitalists have been.
Founders of some of Silicon Valley’s largest companies, including Sergey Brin, Larry Page, Peter Thiel, Mark Zuckerberg and Travis Kalanick, have changed their residencies or announced plans to cut ties with the state in one way or another.
What makes Proposition 40 so dangerously self-destructive is California’s extraordinary dependence upon taxing high-income earners. Over the last two decades, the top 1% of earners have paid approximately 45% of the state’s income taxes.
For that reason, the state’s most respected, nonpartisan authority on policy, the Legislative Analyst’s Office, forecasts short-term benefits but long-term costs:
California will “probably collect tens of billions of dollars from the wealth tax,” according to the LAO. But those gains would likely be temporary.
That’s because the LAO worries that “billionaires may respond to a new wealth tax in ways that reduce their income tax payments. For example, some billionaires may decide to leave California. The income taxes they currently pay to the state also would go away.”
In fact, the LAO projects that billionaires leaving the state would reduce the state’s General Fund revenues by “less than a billion per year.”
But the union that pushed this proposition — Services Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West — wants to gamble.
Its leaders created this to help themselves first and foremost, even at the expense of their typical allies. Opposition to this proposition includes the California Teachers Association, the Association of California School Administrators and the California Professional Firefighters, among several other public and private sector unions. These unions know they’ll suffer when the state’s General Fund takes a hit.
Even the liberal governor of this state is fiercely opposed.
“We can’t let a single advocacy organization, however well-intentioned, write the state’s tax code on its own terms,” said Gov. Gavin Newsom.
We couldn’t agree more.
Self-shackling
To counter Proposition 40, Building a Better California — a political action committee formed earlier this year and backed by Silicon Valley billionaires including Sergey Brin, Vinod Khosla and Eric Scmidt — created two countermeasures, Propositions 41 and 42.
If either Proposition 41 or 42 receives more votes than Proposition 40, the billionaires tax won’t take effect.
The problem is that these two propositions would do far more than nullify the billionaires tax. They would tie the hands of the state far into the future in ways we cannot abide.

Successive waves of federal cuts to California’s safety net are hitting our shores — and hospitals.
H.R. 1 (aka the “One Big Beautiful Bill Act”), the spending plan written by House Republicans and signed into law last year by President Donald Trump, included the largest reductions in U.S. history to food assistance and health care programs. Its intentionally punitive and retaliatory cuts to California’s Medicaid program, Medi-Cal, are projected to cost the state billions of dollars per year and lead to more than a million Californians losing access to health care.

Killing Golden Goose
Proposition 40 risks long-term pain for short-term gain. It’s the ballot equivalent of eating your seed corn.
Here’s how it would work:
Proposition 40 would impose a one-time 5% levy on the net worth of billionaires who were residents of California on January 1. The tax would be due next year, but the state’s 250 or so billionaires could spread the payments out over five years.
Ninety percent of the revenues raised — estimated anywhere between $40 billion to $100 billion, depending on the expert — would fund health care services. The rest would go toward education and food assistance and administration.
What distinguishes this tax isn’t just that it’s targeting a very base of extremely high-net worth individuals but also that it applies retroactively and taxes wealth, not income.
Wealth taxes are unpopular with many economists, including liberal ones, for several reasons:
They can force the sale of productive assets (e.g. stock shares, patents, copyrights, farmland, etc). They’re difficult to administer because determining the value of some intangible assets, unlike income, is more art than a science. And most injuriously, they can encourage capital flight, especially when executed by a state acting alone.
To be sure, the capital hasn’t fled California yet, but the capitalists have been.
Founders of some of Silicon Valley’s largest companies, including Sergey Brin, Larry Page, Peter Thiel, Mark Zuckerberg and Travis Kalanick, have changed their residencies or announced plans to cut ties with the state in one way or another.
What makes Proposition 40 so dangerously self-destructive is California’s extraordinary dependence upon taxing high-income earners. Over the last two decades, the top 1% of earners have paid approximately 45% of the state’s income taxes.

California will “probably collect tens of billions of dollars from the wealth tax,” according to the LAO. But those gains would likely be temporary.

In fact, the LAO projects that billionaires leaving the state would reduce the state’s General Fund revenues by “less than a billion per year.”
But the union that pushed this proposition — Services Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West — wants to gamble.
Its leaders created this to help themselves first and foremost, even at the expense of their typical allies. Opposition to this proposition includes the California Teachers Association, the Association of California School Administrators and the California Professional Firefighters, among several other public and private sector unions. These unions know they’ll suffer when the state’s General Fund takes a hit.
Even the liberal governor of this state is fiercely opposed.
“We can’t let a single advocacy organization, however well-intentioned, write the state’s tax code on its own terms,” said Gov. Gavin Newsom.
We couldn’t agree more.
Self-shackling
To counter Proposition 40, Building a Better California — a political action committee formed earlier this year and backed by Silicon Valley billionaires including Sergey Brin, Vinod Khosla and Eric Scmidt — created two countermeasures, Propositions 41 and 42.
If either Proposition 41 or 42 receives more votes than Proposition 40, the billionaires tax won’t take effect.

I'm checking whether the measure's real effect on retirement accounts is actually as weak as the framing suggests, since that determines how much weight the "it's just about 401(k)s" argument deserves.

I'm checking the factual claims: that Prop 42 is designed to nullify Prop 40, and what the campaign says would happen if Prop 40 wins more votes. Per the Prop 42 campaign spokesperson, even then Prop 42 would still apply to future taxes on personal property and savings, so the billionaire tax would survive while future wealth taxes stay barred.

I'm verifying the key facts now: the measure's title and its core bans on new taxes on personal property and savings, plus its ban on most retroactive state taxes, with the Legislature-enacted exception limited to 365 days.

Next I'm checking the conflict clause, which would void Prop 40 if Prop 42 gets more yes votes, along with the legal-defense provision that funds independent counsel from the General Fund.

Now I'm checking the remaining facts: the LAO's warning that future revenue could be harder to raise, and the current state tax setup, which taxes income from financial assets rather than their ownership. I'm also confirming Prop 40's basics, a one-time 5% tax on billionaires' net worth, with exclusions for real estate, pensions, and most retirement accounts.

I'm checking how the conflict plays out if both measures pass. If Prop 42 gets more yes votes, Prop 40 is void, but if Prop 40 gets more, it's legally unclear how much of 42 would still apply, since its campaign says its ban on future wealth taxes would survive, and courts would have to decide.

Now I'm checking the polling picture, comparing the latest PPIC numbers for Prop 42 and Prop 40 against the earlier September results.

I'm checking the endorsement lists now, with the yes side including Newsom, the state Republican Party, and CalChamber, and the no side including SEIU-UHW, the state Democratic Party, and several major newspapers. I still need to confirm whether CalChamber actually endorsed Prop 42.

Now I'm checking the campaign money: the Prop 42 yes side has raised roughly $128 million, mostly through Brin's Building a Better California group, while the opposition has raised about $22.7 million, mostly from SEIU-UHW's committee.

Now I'm checking the wealth-tax proposals in the legislature: the Chronicle reports that all six introduced since 2019 died before leaving their house of origin, so there's no active bill on the table.

Now I'm checking the retroactivity rules: the measure bars new retroactive taxes, with the only carve-out being Legislature-passed taxes reaching back no more than a year during a governor-declared emergency.

I'm noting how the Budget Center and Holland & Knight describe Prop 42 as limiting future lawmakers' ability to pursue wealth-based taxes, and I'm checking the Peace Officers' view that taxing middle-class retirement accounts is within the realm of possibility.

Now I'm weighing whether the Roth IRA exception matters here: under Prop 40, Roth balances above $10 million would be taxed, so a Yes on 42 vote would also shield those very large accounts, which goes beyond the ordinary 401(k) argument.

I'm noting that Prop 40's Roth IRA provision would tax balances above $10 million, so a Yes on 42 would also shield those very large accounts, which cuts both ways on the "it's just 401(k)s" framing. I'm also checking the election date: the vote is Tuesday, November 3, 2026, with polls open 7 a.m. to 8 p.m.

Next I'm checking how the Yes on 42 campaign's FAQ and retirement-impact page describe the measure, especially whether they acknowledge that it would void Prop 40. I'm also looking at the San Diego Union-Tribune and Mercury News endorsements to compare the strongest arguments on each side.

content.text: No results were posted when I checked, so the vote appears to be still pending. A court also upheld the Attorney General's ballot label for Prop 42 in August. Next I'll read the Yes campaign's FAQ and the two opposing editorial boards, so I can compare their strongest arguments.

Frequently Asked Questions
Prop 42 is a measure on the November 3, 2026 ballot (https://urldefense.proofpoint.com/v2/url?u=https-3A__vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov_2026_general_pdf_prop42-2Dtext-2Dproposed-2Dlaws.pdf&d=DwMGaQ&c=euGZstcaTDllvimEN8b7jXrwqOf-v5A_CdpgnVfiiMM&r=Lbak5eFZHnZSYhftzpqbORUrs1mHGbmgfEVBYVeetqU&m=3Kh86csSe4Cl6q9fcUvr1QX3IGpDHhcugmEJous0LV6L-5TYZP1t6L6mee4OHIHn&s=c3Gqu-OMIDatgK3hnMmB3S2ODmqsGQ0poGtXleReCu8&e=) that protects Californians from double taxation on the money we earn by closing a loophole (https://urldefense.proofpoint.com/v2/url?u=https-3A__voterguide.sos.ca.gov_propositions_42_&d=DwMGaQ&c=euGZstcaTDllvimEN8b7jXrwqOf-v5A_CdpgnVfiiMM&r=Lbak5eFZHnZSYhftzpqbORUrs1mHGbmgfEVBYVeetqU&m=3Kh86csSe4Cl6q9fcUvr1QX3IGpDHhcugmEJous0LV6L-5TYZP1t6L6mee4OHIHn&s=ufUF2OJehlbx--9fM7nvGFw4Qh_D0Cgtj_UKws5-HY0&e=) in California’s Constitution that allows new state taxes on retirement accounts, personal savings, pensions, and other personal property.
Updated October 13, 2026
What is Prop 42 (2026)? (javascript:void(0))
Prop 42, the Retirement & Personal Savings Protection Act of 2026, protects Californians from double taxation on the money we earn (https://urldefense.proofpoint.com/v2/url?u=https-3A__voterguide.sos.ca.gov_propositions_42_&d=DwMGaQ&c=euGZstcaTDllvimEN8b7jXrwqOf-v5A_CdpgnVfiiMM&r=Lbak5eFZHnZSYhftzpqbORUrs1mHGbmgfEVBYVeetqU&m=3Kh86csSe4Cl6q9fcUvr1QX3IGpDHhcugmEJous0LV6L-5TYZP1t6L6mee4OHIHn&s=ufUF2OJehlbx--9fM7nvGFw4Qh_D0Cgtj_UKws5-HY0&e=) by closing a loophole in California’s Constitution that allows new state taxes on retirement accounts, personal savings, pensions, and other personal property.
You already pay income taxes when you earn your money. Proposition 42 (2026) ensures the state cannot tax that same money twice simply because it is sitting in a retirement account or savings account. It also prohibits retroactive taxes (https://urldefense.proofpoint.com/v2/url?u=https-3A__vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov_2026_general_pdf_prop42-2Dtext-2Dproposed-2Dlaws.pdf&d=DwMGaQ&c=euGZstcaTDllvimEN8b7jXrwqOf-v5A_CdpgnVfiiMM&r=Lbak5eFZHnZSYhftzpqbORUrs1mHGbmgfEVBYVeetqU&m=3Kh86csSe4Cl6q9fcUvr1QX3IGpDHhcugmEJous0LV6L-5TYZP1t6L6mee4OHIHn&s=c3Gqu-OMIDatgK3hnMmB3S2ODmqsGQ0poGtXleReCu8&e=) that would change the rules after you’ve already earned and saved.
You earned and saved it. Prop 42 (2026) protects it.
Why is Prop 42 Needed? (javascript:void(0))
California is the third most expensive state (https://urldefense.proofpoint.com/v2/url?u=https-3A__www.cnbc.com_make-2Dit_2025_01_19_most-2Dexpensive-2Dus-2Dstates-2Dto-2Dretire.html&d=DwMGaQ&c=euGZstcaTDllvimEN8b7jXrwqOf-v5A_CdpgnVfiiMM&r=Lbak5eFZHnZSYhftzpqbORUrs1mHGbmgfEVBYVeetqU&m=3Kh86csSe4Cl6q9fcUvr1QX3IGpDHhcugmEJous0LV6L-5TYZP1t6L6mee4OHIHn&s=q3QbdWzqFeD9B_wUx9JL86V-tLjHuGtDqGwUv2vctdw&e=) for retirees. Our high cost of living and high taxes already make it difficult for people to get ahead or to save enough for retirement. A recent survey of Californians found that 73% know someone who has had to delay retirement for financial reasons.
Californians deserve peace of mind that their hard-earned savings will be there when they need them. Yet, California’s Constitution allows the Legislature and special interests to impose new state taxes on retirement accounts and personal savings. It should be illegal for politicians and special interests to tax our retirement and savings. Prop 42 (2026) closes that loophole (https://urldefense.proofpoint.com/v2/url?u=https-3A__vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov_2026_general_pdf_prop42-2Dtext-2Dproposed-2Dlaws.pdf&d=DwMGaQ&c=euGZstcaTDllvimEN8b7jXrwqOf-v5A_CdpgnVfiiMM&r=Lbak5eFZHnZSYhftzpqbORUrs1mHGbmgfEVBYVeetqU&m=3Kh86csSe4Cl6q9fcUvr1QX3IGpDHhcugmEJous0LV6L-5TYZP1t6L6mee4OHIHn&s=c3Gqu-OMIDatgK3hnMmB3S2ODmqsGQ0poGtXleReCu8&e=) and protects retirement, life savings and personal property from new taxes.
Can the Legislature Pass Taxes on Retirement & Life Savings Today? (javascript:void(0))
Yes. California's Constitution currently gives the Legislature the authority to impose taxes on personal property such as retirement accounts, pensions, 401(k)s, IRAs, bank accounts, and other personal savings.
In recent years, lawmakers have introduced five separate bills proposing taxes on retirement savings and other personal property. Although none became law, these attempts underscore that this authority already exists and has been tried repeatedly.
The Legislature should not be able to tax retirement accounts. Prop 42 (2026) provides that protection by closing the loophole in California's Constitution before it can be used to tax retirement savings and personal property.
What Does Prop 42 Protect? (javascript:void(0))
Prop 42 (2026) (https://urldefense.proofpoint.com/v2/url?u=https-3A__voterguide.sos.ca.gov_propositions_42_&d=DwMGaQ&c=euGZstcaTDllvimEN8b7jXrwqOf-v5A_CdpgnVfiiMM&r=Lbak5eFZHnZSYhftzpqbORUrs1mHGbmgfEVBYVeetqU&m=3Kh86csSe4Cl6q9fcUvr1QX3IGpDHhcugmEJous0LV6L-5TYZP1t6L6mee4OHIHn&s=ufUF2OJehlbx--9fM7nvGFw4Qh_D0Cgtj_UKws5-HY0&e=) protects retirement accounts, including 401(k)s, pensions, IRAs, and other retirement plans. It also protects personal savings accounts and other personal property that could otherwise be subject to new state taxes.
How Would a Tax on Retirement Savings Affect My 401(k)? (javascript:void(0))
Even a small annual tax on retirement savings could reduce both the value of your retirement savings and the investment growth that helps build retirement security over time.
A recent economic analysis (https://urldefense.proofpoint.com/v2/url?u=https-3A__www.morningstar.com_news_pr-2Dnewswire_20260929la57497_10000-2Da-2Dyear-2Dtax-2Don-2Dretirement-2Dnew-2Dreport-2Dshows-2Dhow-2Deven-2Da-2Dsmall-2Dtax-2Don-2Dyour-2Dretirement-2Dcan-2Dhave-2Dhuge-2Dimpact-2Don-2Dyour-2Dfinances&d=DwMGaQ&c=euGZstcaTDllvimEN8b7jXrwqOf-v5A_CdpgnVfiiMM&r=Lbak5eFZHnZSYhftzpqbORUrs1mHGbmgfEVBYVeetqU&m=3Kh86csSe4Cl6q9fcUvr1QX3IGpDHhcugmEJous0LV6L-5TYZP1t6L6mee4OHIHn&s=ZTMu5TxB_roUrtTd3dWzB9ulnZEAslHk2U4ENj0Fggc&e=) found that even a 1% tax on retirement could cause middle-class Californians to face annual tax bills of up to $10,000 and have to work up to seven additional years before retiring. Prop 42 (2026) protects 401(k)s and other retirement savings from new state taxes that would chip into retirement savings or force Californians to delay retirement.
Does Prop 42 Impact Existing Programs or Funding? (javascript:void(0))
No. Prop 42 (2026) does not reduce existing funding for schools, public safety, healthcare, transportation, or other state programs. It simply prohibits new state taxes on retirement savings and other personal property. Existing revenue sources and funding formulas remain unchanged.
Does Prop 42 Only Protect Wealthy Californians? (javascript:void(0))
No. Prop 42 (2026) protects everyone who works and saves for retirement, including teachers, firefighters, police officers, veterans, retirees, small business owners, and middle-class families. If you have retirement savings or personal savings, Prop 42 (2026) protects you.
Who Supports Prop 42? (javascript:void(0))
Prop 42 (2026) is supported by a broad coalition of seniors, firefighters, veterans, building trades workers, small businesses, and working families who believe Californians should not pay taxes twice on the money they earn and save. This includes the California Professional Firefighters, California Senior Alliance, AMVETS, Dept. of California, State Building and Construction Trades Council of California, Peace Officers Research Association of California, and the California Small Business Association.
Privacy Policy (https://yesonprop42.org/privacy-policy/)
Paid for by Yes on 42 – Protect Retirement & Life Savings, a coalition of retirees, blue-collar workers, seniors, veterans, small businesses & taxpayers. Committee’s top funders:
Building a Better California & Peace Officers Research Association of California.

By The Editorial Board (https://www.sandiegouniontribune.com/author/the-editorial-board/) | opinion@scng.com (mailto:opinion@scng.com)
PUBLISHED: September 21, 2026 at 2:39 PM PDT | UPDATED: September 21, 2026 at 2:56 PM PDT

The most hotly debated initiative on the November ballot is Proposition 40, which would impose a 5% tax on the wealth of California billionaires. As this Editorial Board opined (https://www.ocregister.com/2026/09/13/endorsement-no-on-proposition-40s-reckless-wealth-tax/) in our opposition, the union-created Billionaire Tax Act would send a dangerous message to current and future entrepreneurs, and “have a chilling effect on investment.”
But two closely related measures, Propositions 41 and 42 (https://www.bakersfield.com/opinion/our-view/our-view-vote-no-on-propositions-40-41-42-tax-propositions-hurt-state-californians/article_1c8492b8-5fb9-4897-9f1c-c9ba56460e0d.amp.html) , have received much less attention — partly because they’re so complicated. By adding related measures to the ballot, opponents of Prop. 40 are hoping that voters approve one of these alternatives that will derail Prop. 40. Because these two measures have elements that contradict Prop. 40, the one that gets the highest vote totals (if voters OK them all) would go into effect.
Adding similar-sounding measures also muddies the waters, thus increasing the likelihood that confused voters vote “no” on all of them — thus accomplishing the main goal of stopping the billionaires’ tax. But our goal isn’t to map out political strategies (https://www.pbs.org/wgbh/americanexperience/features/nash-game/) . It’s a worthy effort to try to stop a disastrous new tax scheme.
Besides their intended purpose of blocking Prop. 40, the measures could protect taxpayers for years to come.
Specifically, Prop. 41 would require one-time audits of programs that any proposed special taxes would fund. Those audits, which must be completed before the initiative appears on the ballot, would be required to identify ways that such programs could cut annual costs by 10%, per an analysis (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=41&year=2026) from the Legislative Analyst’s Office.
While Prop. 40 exempts itself from state spending limits, Prop. 41 also requires new special-tax revenues to count toward the Gann Limit (https://www.sheehystrategygroup.com/news/2026/3/9/californias-state-appropriations-limit-gann-limit) — the 1979 constitutional amendment that caps the revenue the state can spend each year. The state has passed a number of workarounds over the years, but applying new revenues to this formula would potentially require the return of certain additional tax revenues to taxpayers (https://www.yesonprop41.org/about-prop41) and the earmarking of revenues to infrastructure.
Prop. 42 is more straightforward. Per theLAO (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=42&year=2026), the initiative prohibits “new taxes on the ownership of financial assets or other personal property.” California doesn’t currently tax the ownership of financial assets and only taxes personal property in a limited way (e.g., vehicle license fees), but the measure’s passage “could make it somewhat harder for the state to raise taxes.” It also limits imposition of retroactive taxes.
So would the Editorial Board support these measures even if they were standalone initiatives? The answers are unequivocal: Yes and yes.

Successive waves of federal cuts to California’s safety net are hitting our shores — and hospitals.
H.R. 1 (aka the “One Big Beautiful Bill Act”), the spending plan written by House Republicans and signed into law last year by President Donald Trump, included the largest reductions in U.S. history to food assistance and health care programs. However, this measure is the wrong solution to a real problem.
We advise California voters to reject short-sighted, self-sabotaging Proposition 40.
And we recommend they reject equally myopic Propositions 41 and 42 — countermeasures that would not only nullify the billionaires tax but senselessly shackle the state’s fiscal future.
Killing Golden Goose
Proposition 40 risks long-term pain for short-term gain. It’s the ballot equivalent of eating your seed corn.
Here’s how it would work:
Proposition 40 would impose a one-time 5% levy on the net worth of billionaires who were residents of California on January 1. The tax would be due next year, but the state’s 250 or so billionaires could spread the payments out over five years.
Ninety percent of the revenues raised — estimated anywhere between $40 billion to $100 billion, depending on the expert — would fund health care services. The rest would go toward education and food assistance and administration.
What distinguishes this tax isn’t just that it’s targeting a very base of extremely high-net worth individuals but also that it applies retroactively and taxes wealth, not income.
Wealth taxes are unpopular with many economists, including liberal ones, for several reasons:
They can force the sale of productive assets (e.g. stock shares, patents, copyrights, farmland, etc). They’re difficult to administer because determining the value of some intangible assets, unlike income, is more art than a science. And most injuriously, they can encourage capital flight, especially when executed by a state acting alone.
To be sure, the capital hasn’t fled California yet, but the capitalists have been.
Founders of some of Silicon Valley’s largest companies, including Sergey Brin, Larry Page, Peter Thiel, Mark Zuckerberg and Travis Kalanick, have changed their residencies or announced plans to cut ties with the state in one way or another.
What makes Proposition 40 so dangerously self-destructive is California’s extraordinary dependence upon taxing high-income earners. Over the last two decades, the top 1% of earners have paid approximately 45% of the state’s income taxes.
For that reason, the state’s most respected, nonpartisan authority on policy, the Legislative Analyst’s Office, forecasts short-term benefits but long-term costs:
California will “probably collect tens of billions of dollars from the wealth tax,” according to the LAO. But those gains would likely be temporary.
That’s because the LAO worries that “billionaires may respond to a new wealth tax in ways that reduce their income tax payments. For example, some billionaires may decide to leave California. The income taxes they currently pay to the state also would go away.”
In fact, the LAO projects that billionaires leaving the state would reduce the state’s General Fund revenues by “less than a billion per year.”
But the union that pushed this proposition — Services Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West — wants to gamble.
Its leaders created this to help themselves first and foremost, even at the expense of their typical allies. Opposition to this proposition includes the California Teachers Association, the Association of California School Administrators and the California Professional Firefighters, among several other public and private sector unions. These unions know they’ll suffer when the state’s General Fund takes a hit.
Even the liberal governor of this state is fiercely opposed.
“We can’t let a single advocacy organization, however well-intentioned, write the state’s tax code on its own terms,” said Gov. Gavin Newsom.
We couldn’t agree more.
Self-shackling
To counter Proposition 40, Building a Better California — a political action committee formed earlier this year and backed by Silicon Valley billionaires including Sergey Brin, Vinod Khosla and Eric Scmidt — created two countermeasures, Propositions 41 and 42.
If either Proposition 41 or 42 receives more votes than Proposition 40, the billionaires tax won’t take effect.
The problem is that these two propositions would do far more than nullify the billionaires tax. They would tie the hands of the state far into the future in ways we cannot abide.
Proposition 41
This initiative’s requirement for more audits could be valuable. It would mandate that the State Auditor scrutinize special taxes before they appear on the ballot as well as ongoing programs funded by special taxes. The LAO sees possible savings if the auditor’s recommendations are followed.
However, the problem with Proposition 41 is its second provision. It would prevent any new special taxes from being excluded from the “Gann Limit” — a strict state spending cap enacted in 1979. That means that voters could approve a new tax to address a pressing public need, only to discover that the state cannot spend the money it collects without being constrained by a constitutional limit written half a century ago.

assistantMessageEvent.content:
This turns on a values question: should California be able to tax wealth in the future? I won't pick a side on that for you, but here's the yes/no version:

- **Yes** if you want the state permanently barred from new taxes on owning wealth, including taxes aimed only at the very rich, and from most retroactive taxes.
- **No** if you want to keep those options open, including if you back Prop 40's billionaire tax.

**What it does**
- Bars new state taxes on owning personal property: financial assets, retirement accounts, pensions, business interests, intellectual property, and personal belongings. It applies at any wealth level. It doesn't change income or capital gains taxes, real estate taxes, or taxes already in place.
- Bars new retroactive taxes, including taxes based on residency before the tax takes effect. The one exception covers Legislature-passed taxes that reach back no more than 365 days, only during a governor-declared emergency, with revenue limited to that emergency.
- Because it's a constitutional amendment, only voters could change it later.
- If it gets more yes votes than Prop 40, Prop 40 is void, even if Prop 40 wins a majority.

**The retirement argument**
- Supporters say lawmakers keep introducing wealth-tax bills, so the protection belongs in the constitution. Six such proposals have been introduced since 2019, and none got out of its house of origin. The two I checked started at $30 million (AB 2088, 2019) and $50 million (AB 259, 2023) in net worth.
- I found no active proposal to tax 401(k)s or pensions. Prop 40 exempts most retirement accounts, though it would tax Roth IRA balances over $10 million.
- "Double taxation" fits after-tax savings best. Traditional 401(k)s and IRAs are generally taxed when withdrawn.
- The bigger long-run effect is permanence: any future wealth tax would need a new constitutional amendment.

**Trade-offs**
- The nonpartisan Legislative Analyst says it could make taxes "somewhat harder" to raise and reduce future revenue, by an unclear amount.
- The California Budget & Policy Center says it would limit options for taxing wealthy households. The SF Chronicle says the retroactivity ban could create legal complications.

**Politics**
- Backed by Gov. Newsom, the CalChamber, the California Taxpayers Association, firefighters, and building trades, and endorsed by the San Diego Union-Tribune and OC Register. Opposed by SEIU-UHW (Prop 40's sponsor), the state Democratic Party, the state labor federation, and the SF Chronicle, Sacramento Bee, and Mercury News.
- Most of the roughly $128 million raised for it came from Building a Better California, which is funded largely by Sergey Brin and other billionaires and also opposes Prop 40.
- Each side's main pitch skips part of the picture. The Yes side's 401(k) message doesn't convey how broad the ban is. The No side's "billionaire trick" message doesn't address whether a permanent ban is good policy.
- PPIC's October poll: 51% yes, 47% no.

**If Prop 40 is your deciding issue**
- To keep Prop 40 from being blocked, vote No on 41 and 42.
- If both 40 and 42 pass and 40 gets more votes, courts would have to sort out the conflict. The Prop 42 campaign says its ban would still cover future wealth taxes.

**Bottom line on the facts:** the retirement rationale is weaker than the ads suggest, and the measure is broader than its title. Whether a permanent ban is worth it is your call.

I checked the measure's full text, the LAO analysis, polling, and coverage from both sides. I found no results yet, so the vote appears to still be pending. Election Day is Nov. 3.

content.text:
This turns on a values question: should California be able to tax wealth in the future? I won't pick a side on that for you, but here's the yes/no version:

- **Yes** if you want the state permanently barred from new taxes on owning wealth, including taxes aimed only at the very rich, and from most retroactive taxes.
- **No** if you want to keep those options open, including if you back Prop 40's billionaire tax.

**What it does**
- Bars new state taxes on owning personal property: financial assets, retirement accounts, pensions, business interests, intellectual property, and personal belongings. It applies at any wealth level. It doesn't change income or capital gains taxes, real estate taxes, or taxes already in place.
- Bars new retroactive taxes, including taxes based on residency before the tax takes effect. The one exception covers Legislature-passed taxes that reach back no more than 365 days, only during a governor-declared emergency, with revenue limited to that emergency.
- Because it's a constitutional amendment, only voters could change it later.
- If it gets more yes votes than Prop 40, Prop 40 is void, even if Prop 40 wins a majority.

**The retirement argument**
- Supporters say lawmakers keep introducing wealth-tax bills, so the protection belongs in the constitution. Six such proposals have been introduced since 2019, and none got out of its house of origin. The two I checked started at $30 million (AB 2088, 2019) and $50 million (AB 259, 2023) in net worth.
- I found no active proposal to tax 401(k)s or pensions. Prop 40 exempts most retirement accounts, though it would tax Roth IRA balances over $10 million.
- "Double taxation" fits after-tax savings best. Traditional 401(k)s and IRAs are generally taxed when withdrawn.
- The bigger long-run effect is permanence: any future wealth tax would need a new constitutional amendment.

**Trade-offs**
- The nonpartisan Legislative Analyst says it could make taxes "somewhat harder" to raise and reduce future revenue, by an unclear amount.
- The California Budget & Policy Center says it would limit options for taxing wealthy households. The SF Chronicle says the retroactivity ban could create legal complications.

**Politics**
- Backed by Gov. Newsom, the CalChamber, the California Taxpayers Association, firefighters, and building trades, and endorsed by the San Diego Union-Tribune and OC Register. Opposed by SEIU-UHW (Prop 40's sponsor), the state Democratic Party, the state labor federation, and the SF Chronicle, Sacramento Bee, and Mercury News.
- Most of the roughly $128 million raised for it came from Building a Better California, which is funded largely by Sergey Brin and other billionaires and also opposes Prop 40.
- Each side's main pitch skips part of the picture. The Yes side's 401(k) message doesn't convey how broad the ban is. The No side's "billionaire trick" message doesn't address whether a permanent ban is good policy.
- PPIC's October poll: 51% yes, 47% no.

**If Prop 40 is your deciding issue**
- To keep Prop 40 from being blocked, vote No on 41 and 42.
- If both 40 and 42 pass and 40 gets more votes, courts would have to sort out the conflict. The Prop 42 campaign says its ban would still cover future wealth taxes.

**Bottom line on the facts:** the retirement rationale is weaker than the ads suggest, and the measure is broader than its title. Whether a permanent ban is worth it is your call.

I checked the measure's full text, the LAO analysis, polling, and coverage from both sides. I found no results yet, so the vote appears to still be pending. Election Day is Nov. 3.

content.text:
This turns on a values question: should California be able to tax wealth in the future? I won't pick a side on that for you, but here's the yes/no version:

- **Yes** if you want the state permanently barred from new taxes on owning wealth, including taxes aimed only at the very rich, and from most retroactive taxes.
- **No** if you want to keep those options open, including if you back Prop 40's billionaire tax.

**What it does**
- Bars new state taxes on owning personal property: financial assets, retirement accounts, pensions, business interests, intellectual property, and personal belongings. It applies at any wealth level. It doesn't change income or capital gains taxes, real estate taxes, or taxes already in place.
- Bars new retroactive taxes, including taxes based on residency before the tax takes effect. The one exception covers Legislature-passed taxes that reach back no more than 365 days, only during a governor-declared emergency, with revenue limited to that emergency.
- Because it's a constitutional amendment, only voters could change it later.
- If it gets more yes votes than Prop 40, Prop 40 is void, even if Prop 40 wins a majority.

**The retirement argument**
- Supporters say lawmakers keep introducing wealth-tax bills, so the protection belongs in the constitution. Six such proposals have been introduced since 2019, and none got out of its house of origin. The two I checked started at $30 million (AB 2088, 2019) and $50 million (AB 259, 2023) in net worth.
- I found no active proposal to tax 401(k)s or pensions. Prop 40 exempts most retirement accounts, though it would tax Roth IRA balances over $10 million.
- "Double taxation" fits after-tax savings best. Traditional 401(k)s and IRAs are generally taxed when withdrawn.
- The bigger long-run effect is permanence: any future wealth tax would need a new constitutional amendment.

**Trade-offs**
- The nonpartisan Legislative Analyst says it could make taxes "somewhat harder" to raise and reduce future revenue, by an unclear amount.
- The California Budget & Policy Center says it would limit options for taxing wealthy households. The SF Chronicle says the retroactivity ban could create legal complications.

**Politics**
- Backed by Gov. Newsom, the CalChamber, the California Taxpayers Association, firefighters, and building trades, and endorsed by the San Diego Union-Tribune and OC Register. Opposed by SEIU-UHW (Prop 40's sponsor), the state Democratic Party, the state labor federation, and the SF Chronicle, Sacramento Bee, and Mercury News.
- Most of the roughly $128 million raised for it came from Building a Better California, which is funded largely by Sergey Brin and other billionaires and also opposes Prop 40.
- Each side's main pitch skips part of the picture. The Yes side's 401(k) message doesn't convey how broad the ban is. The No side's "billionaire trick" message doesn't address whether a permanent ban is good policy.
- PPIC's October poll: 51% yes, 47% no.

**If Prop 40 is your deciding issue**
- To keep Prop 40 from being blocked, vote No on 41 and 42.
- If both 40 and 42 pass and 40 gets more votes, courts would have to sort out the conflict. The Prop 42 campaign says its ban would still cover future wealth taxes.

**Bottom line on the facts:** the retirement rationale is weaker than the ads suggest, and the measure is broader than its title. Whether a permanent ban is worth it is your call.

I checked the measure's full text, the LAO analysis, polling, and coverage from both sides. I found no results yet, so the vote appears to still be pending. Election Day is Nov. 3.

Proposition 42: Personal Property and State Taxes
Proposition 42: Personal Property and State Taxes
Proposition 42: Prohibits New State Personal Property Taxes And Certain Retroactive State Taxes. Initiative Constitutional Amendment.
Additional Titles
Retirement and Personal Savings Protection Act
Summary
Proposition 42 was placed on the ballot by petition signatures to amend the California Constitution. It began as Initiative #25-0039A1 (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/25-0039A1%20%28CA%20Residency%20Act%20%29.pdf) , filed with the California Attorney General’s Office. Prop. 42 amends the California Constitution by adding Article VIII, Sections 1 through 9.
Under Proposition 42, new taxes on the ownership of financial assets (e.g. pensions, stocks, or retirement accounts) and tangible or intangible personal property would not be allowed.
Proposition 42 also prohibits retroactive taxes that authorize a tax on conduct, activities, or status that occurred or was present prior to the effective date of the state law or constitution. A retroactive tax is one that applies to things that happened in the past. An example is a tax on money someone earned two years ago.
If Proposition 42 receives more “yes” votes than Proposition 40 (Billionaire Wealth Tax) on this same ballot, then Proposition 40 could be stopped from becoming law even if it gets yes votes from a majority of voters. This is because the courts could find that Proposition 42 conflicts with Proposition 40.
F iscal Impact
(Summary of Legislative Analyst's Estimate of Net State and Local Government Fiscal Impact)
Proposition 42 restricts the options the state has to raise taxes in the future, making it somewhat harder to raise revenue through taxes. It is unclear how much future revenues would be reduced.
What your vote means (LAO Analysis)
A YES vote on this measure means: The state could not establish new taxes on the ownership of financial assets or other personal property.
A NO vote on this measure means: The state would continue to have the option to establish new taxes on the ownership of financial assets or other personal property.

Issue Brief
What Would Proposition 42 Mean for California?
Understanding the Prohibition on Taxing Certain Assets and Enacting Retroactive Taxes
September 2026 | By Kayla Kitson (https://calbudgetcenter.org/people/kayla-kitson/)
Print Issue Brief
key takeaway
Prop. 42 would prohibit new taxes on the ownership of certain assets as well as taxes that apply retroactively. The primary intent of the measure is to invalidate Prop. 40 — the one-time billionaire tax measure also appearing on the November ballot — if it receives more votes, and it would also create new barriers to raising progressive state revenue in the future to adequately meet the needs of Californians.
What Would Prop. 42 Do?
Prop. 42 would amend the state Constitution to prohibit taxes on the ownership of certain assets and on certain retroactive taxes.
Prohibition on New Taxes on Assets
Prop. 42 would prohibit the imposition of any new state tax — enacted on or after January 1, 2026 — on the ownership of financial assets (such as bank accounts, stocks, bonds, or mutual funds), retirement accounts, interests in businesses, intellectual property, and other personal property (such as vehicles, jewelry, artwork, and other movable, physical property).
Prohibition on Retroactive Taxes
Prop. 42 would prohibit the imposition of new retroactive taxes, specifically any tax that is based on “conduct, activities, or a status” that preceded the effective date of the tax. The measure also explicitly prohibits taxes based on someone’s residency status prior to the tax going into effect. An exception would be made for retroactive taxes in cases where the revenues would be used to respond to a governor-declared emergency and the tax does not apply retroactively for more than one year before the effective date.
What Would Prop. 42 Mean for Californians and the State Budget?
The primary intent of Prop. 42 is to invalidate Prop. 40 (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/billionaire-tax-explained-what-proposition-40-would-mean-for-california/), which would create a one-time tax on the wealth of billionaires. The tax would apply retroactively to billionaires who were California residents on January 1, 2026 and would apply to financial assets like stocks and bonds and other types of assets that would put it in direct conflict with Prop. 42’s prohibition of such taxes — though Prop. 40 would exclude retirement accounts, which is a key focus of Prop. 42. If both measures were to pass and Prop. 42 received more votes, Prop. 40 would likely be invalidated.
But the measure would also have more far-reaching consequences by making it harder for state leaders to raise revenues from wealthy households to effectively meet the needs of Californians and to quickly adapt to changing circumstances.
This would come at a time when California is facing challenges on multiple fronts — the consequences of the steep federal cuts to health care and food assistance enacted in H.R. 1 (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/timeline-of-funding-cuts-to-medi-cal-and-calfresh-in-california/), the sustained high poverty rate (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/poverty-in-california-remains-steady-among-the-highest-in-the-nation/), the ongoing housing affordability and homelessness crises, and rising costs of maintaining current services due to inflation and an aging population. Addressing these issues and ensuring California communities can thrive will require the state to substantially raise ongoing revenues (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/building-an-affordable-california-requires-public-investment/).
While Prop. 42 would reduce the options state policymakers have to increase revenues, California voters may still be able to amend the state Constitution in the future to allow a new tax on assets or one that applied retroactively. However, legal challenges are possible and there is no absolute certainty on how courts would rule.
Impacts of Prohibition on Taxing Assets
Currently, the ownership of assets is generally not taxed in California, with the exception of local property taxes on real estate — already subject to strict constitutional limits under Prop. 13 (1978) — and some types of personal property including boats, planes, and business equipment, as well as state vehicle license fees.
While the state does not currently tax (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/billionaire-tax-explained-what-proposition-40-would-mean-for-california/#h-what-is-the-difference-between-income-and-wealth) the ownership of financial assets, business interests, or other intangible assets, it is not constitutionally barred from doing so. Prop. 42 would enshrine this prohibition in the state Constitution, which would prevent state leaders from creating wealth-based taxes in the future. This would limit the options policymakers have to raise progressive revenue to maintain and improve state services that support Californians in staying healthy, housed, and economically secure.
While most Californians hold assets in some form, such as checking or savings accounts, some types of assets are far more likely to be held by wealthy households. For example, about two-thirds of Californians in the top 25% of the wealth distribution hold stocks, bonds, or mutual funds, compared to only 9% of Californians in the bottom 25%, according to an analysis by the Public Policy Institute of California (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/0525ttr-appendix.pdf).
Current federal and state tax policies allow some large wealth increases to never be taxed. California — like the federal government — only taxes the income people receive when they sell their assets, but does not tax the growth in value of assets they hold onto. This growth is known as an unrealized capital gain, and for very wealthy households, unrealized capital gains make up a large share of their total wealth. Some wealthy people may even be able to avoid paying income taxes entirely in some years by not taking a salary, not selling any stocks or other assets, and simply borrowing against their wealth to pay their bills.
Additionally, if someone holds onto assets until their death, their heirs do not have to pay any tax on the gain due to a provision in both federal and state law known as “stepped-up basis,” estimated to cost California around $5 billion each year.
For these reasons, broadly prohibiting state leaders from enacting any new taxes on assets would narrow the options available to ensure that the wealthiest Californians pay their fair share to support the services that benefit residents across the state.
Impacts of Prohibition on Retroactive Taxes
Many federal and state tax law changes have modest retroactivity periods, such as looking back to the beginning of a tax year. This has the benefit of reducing taxpayers’ ability to engage in activities to avoid or evade the tax before it goes into effect, which would reduce the revenue potential. Looking back to the start of the current tax year can also more immediately raise revenues when there are urgent needs.
Broadly prohibiting retroactive taxation would hamstring the ability of state leaders to enact effective and timely tax policy changes that raise revenues needed to meet the needs of Californians.
Who Supports and Opposes Prop. 42?
The top contributor to the Prop. 41 campaign is a group called “Building a Better California,” which is largely funded (https://cal-access.sos.ca.gov/Campaign/Committees/Detail.aspx?id=1486767&view=received) by Google cofounder Sergey Brin and other billionaires. This group is also opposing Prop. 40 and supporting Prop. 41 (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/what-would-proposition-41-mean-for-california/). The measure is also endorsed by the California Republican Party, the California Chamber of Commerce, the California Taxpayers Association, the California Professional Firefighters, and the State Building & Construction Trades Council of California.
There is no official opposition campaign for Prop. 41, but prominent opponents include the Service Employees International Union – United Health Workers West (SEIU-UHW) — the main proponent of the Prop. 40 billionaire tax measure — as well as other labor groups including the California Federation of Teachers and the California Federation of Labor Unions. The California Democratic Party and the League of Women Voters are also opposed.

Photo by Jeff Chiu, AP Photo IN SUMMARY Prop. 40 opponents say the billionaire tax allows lawmakers to change the measure with a two-thirds vote. They warn it opens the door to future wealth taxes on everyday Californians. This is only partially true. Follow the election results in California: Sign up for our newsletter (https://calmatters.org/subscribe-to-calmatters/california-election-newsletter/) to receive alerts when the contests for governor, Prop. 40, insurance commissioner and other key results are called. Opponents of Proposition 40 have a message for voters: Don’t be fooled. The billionaire tax is a “Trojan horse” for new taxes on all Californians, ads proclaim (https://www.facebook.com/ads/library/?active_status=active&ad_type=all&country=US&id=1362825008785008&is_targeted_country=false&media_type=all&search_type=page&sort_data[mode]=total_impressions&sort_data[direction]=desc). But is that true? Tucked into the initiative is language granting the Legislature authority to amend the tax by a two-thirds vote “if the statute is consistent with and furthers the purposes of the 2026 Billionaire Tax Act.” Opponents argue lawmakers and a future governor could, with the stroke of a pen, expand the wealth tax to people with far less than $1 billion. In a high-tax state, that argument could hold a lot of sway with voters. Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West put Prop. 40 on the ballot; the initiative would levy a one-time, 5% tax on billionaire’s assets. The union rejects the premise of the ad. It says the tax is limited to billionaires and any legislative amendment would have to hew closely to that purpose. Dave Regan, president of SEIU-UHW, said opponents’ ads are pure scare tactics. “The billionaire tax is a tax on billionaires. Period. If you’re not a billionaire, you don’t pay the tax,” Regan said in a statement to CalMatters. Rob Lapsley, president of the California Business Roundtable, the group that paid for the ad, said the message was meant to highlight the policy implications of a wealth tax and the power Prop. 40 gives lawmakers. “Californians deserve to understand those issues and what they could mean for taxpayers and the state’s economy,” Lapsley said in a statement. A separate, billionaire-backed group opposed to Prop. 40 has also said the initiative “gives politicians the power to expand the tax to anyone.” The truth lies somewhere in between. California courts have given lawmakers real authority to amend laws created by ballot initiatives if the original text of the initiative permits it. However, that power is not unlimited and the measure includes language restricting future legislative changes, said Michael Colantuono, an attorney with expertise in state election law. Opponents’ ads also don’t mention that Prop. 40 writes the tax into the state Constitution, not just state law, so expanding it would likely require another trip to the ballot. Legislative authority Legal experts agree that if Prop. 40 passes, lawmakers would be able to make certain amendments without taking it back to voters. Sign up for free Δ The state Constitution (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CONS§ionNum=SEC.%2010.&article=II) allows the Legislature to amend a ballot initiative without another vote if the initiative permits it. That’s a relatively common clause in ballot measures, and Prop. 40 includes it. Megan Jones, a tax attorney at Holland & Knight, said proponents’ claims that the tax could never be changed are disingenuous. “If it’s going to further the purposes, then they could,” Jones said. For example, voters passed the Political Reform Act, which governs campaign finance and lobbying rules, in 1974 and lawmakers have amended it almost continually since (https://www.fppc.ca.gov/the-law/the-political-reform-act/). Similarly, lawmakers have amended the Mental Health Services Act, a voter-approved 1% income tax on millionaires, 10 times since its passage in 2004. None of those amendments adjusted the tax rate. Most recently, lawmakers voted to substantially alter how the state spends mental health money and raise additional bond funds. Those changes went back to voters in 2024 as Proposition 1 (https://calmatters.org/health/mental-health/2025/06/prop-1-mental-health-awards/). But there isn’t always a clear line for when voters need to approve changes, experts say. “It is common for the Legislature to make amendments,” Colantuono said. “It is (also) common for there to be disputes about those amendments.” ‘Furthers the purposes of’ “Ultimately, it ends up in court,” said Chris Parker, a principal tax attorney at the firm Baker Tilly. The California Supreme Court ruled in a 1995 case (https://law.justia.com/cases/california/supreme-court/4th/11/1243.html) that the Legislature may amend voter-approved laws if the changes can be interpreted as furthering voters’ original goals “by any reasonable construction” — giving lawmakers broad latitude. In 2021, the state Supreme Court held that the Legislature appropriately amended Proposition 57 (https://law.justia.com/cases/california/supreme-court/2021/s259011.html), a criminal justice reform measure, by barring the transferring of minors under 16 to adult court. Justices cited the 1995 case, noting that “a strong presumption of constitutionality supports the Legislature’s acts.” Still, the language of the proposition matters. A few years earlier, in 2019, the Third District Court of Appeal held that a legislative attempt to allow public funding of political campaigns (https://www4.courts.ca.gov/opinions/archive/C086334.PDF) “directly conflicts with a primary purpose” of the Political Reform Act. Lawmakers responded by passing a new bill (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260SB42) asking voters to weigh in directly — it appears on this year’s ballot as Proposition 4. Judges look at two things, Coluantuono said: what reasonable voters thought they were approving, and whether later legislative changes helped that goal, or got in the way. Certain provisions of Prop. 40 would make it difficult for lawmakers to expand the tax beyond billionaires. The 1995 case established that courts may weigh the language of a ballot measure, arguments printed in the voter guide, and historical context when deciding whether change is consistent with voter intent. Prop. 40’s purpose and intent section (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop40-text-proposed-laws.pdf) says the measure is meant to support healthcare and education “by raising revenue from a one-time tax on billionaire wealth” — referencing billionaire wealth three times. The voter guide arguments similarly target “approximately 200 California billionaires.” “They could probably adjust the structure of the tax in marginal ways, but what they couldn’t do is make it a more than a one-time tax, and they probably couldn’t lower the threshold on wealth,” Coluantuono said. Opponents contend lawmakers could interpret the purpose of the act far more broadly, and a court would agree. They point to the first listed purpose of the initiative that says the tax is meant to “protect access to high quality, equitable health care, and to support funding for kindergarten through grade fourteen public education and food assistance programs.” Opponents also say the proposal gives the Legislature the authority to change all parts of the initiative, including the constitutional provisions. “Prop 40’s findings and statement of purpose and intent were carefully crafted to ensure that extending the tax to non-billionaires would be consistent with the measure,” said Kurt Oneto, a lawyer for the No on 40 campaign, in a statement. Experts said the question would likely come down to how a court read the act’s purposes. A separate concern: how do you prove wealth? Should Prop. 40 pass, it would create an entirely new tax structure in California — one that assigns a value to very wealthy people’s investments, public and private businesses, as well as personal property such as art or car collections. Valuing something like a tech startup that hasn’t produced a product or gone public could prove especially difficult, Parker said. “The excise tax that’s being proposed here is on potential,” he said. “The question then is, if we open the door to taxing potential, when does that stop?” Lawmakers have periodically tried to pass wealth taxes, but the bills quickly stalled. This marks the first time voters will directly decide on one, making Prop. 40 a crucial test of how much appetite Californians have for his kind of tax structure. Jones said the bigger worry isn’t the tax itself, but other taxes that could follow. “It’s a slippery slope,” she said. Coluantuono said it would still be politically risky for lawmakers to try to implement a wealth tax on everyday Californians, but history shows temporary taxes have more than once become permanent. “When we get a revenue stream in the government and we start spending it on services that people value… there’s tremendous political pressure to prevent the sunset,” he said. Billionaire tax explained: What you need to know about Prop. 40
by
Jeanne Kuang (https://calmatters.org/author/jeanne-kuang/) and Kristen Hwang (https://calmatters.org/author/kristen-hwang/)

In summary
Proposition 40 would levy a one-time tax on billionaires. Some say the initiative opens the door to tax flight and more aggressive taxation. Others say there’s no way to predict the outcome.
Follow the election results in California: Sign up for our newsletter (https://calmatters.org/subscribe-to-calmatters/california-election-newsletter/) to receive alerts when the contests for governor, Prop. 40, insurance commissioner and other key results are called.
Proposition 40 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-40-billionaire-tax/), also known as the billionaire tax, is the most contentious fight on Californians’ ballots this November.
The proposal to impose a one-time asset tax on the net worth of the state’s approximately 200 billionaires has divided Democrats, galvanized progressives and sparked fierce pushback from business groups and the state’s wealthy tech sector. Google co-founder Sergey Brin has poured $102 million into the campaign against the measure — including two countermeasures, Propositions 41 and 42 (https://calmatters.org/health/2026/09/california-wealth-tax-prop-40-41-42/) — and is among a handful of billionaires who have moved residences or business assets out of the state in an attempt to avoid the proposed tax. In total, opponents have raised more than $205 million to stop Prop. 40, according to campaign finance records.
It would also set up an entirely new system of taxes in a state that doesn’t traditionally tax wealth. That would be challenging to implement and experts say is sure to invite litigation. Here are some common questions and answers about how the measure would work.
How would the state assess the tax?
Aside from local taxes on real estate and some business equipment, California isn’t in the business of valuing and taxing personal property.
Prop. 40 would require the state, within six months, to create a way to assess the value of a wide range of holdings: billionaires’ stock, investment accounts and business interests, but also their art collections, wine vaults, cars and anything else that stores wealth.
“I have a client who has a machine gun collection,” said Jon Feldhammer, a San Francisco tax attorney who said he is advising several clients who would be or believe they could be subject to the billionaire tax.
The definition of wealth and property has to be broad to close possible loopholes, said Kirk Stark, a UCLA tax law professor.
“Otherwise there would be a very simple workaround, which is, if there’s something that’s exempt then you know there would be an incentive to just shift wealth from one form to another,” Stark said.
Ensuring those subject to the tax aren’t underreporting their assets would require the state’s Franchise Tax Board to hire more people for appraisals and auditing, Stark said.
“It can be done,” he said. “But it’s going to take a huge investment of resources to actually pull it off.”
Franchise Tax Board spokesperson Andrew LePage declined to say how many staff the agency would need to implement Prop. 40. Currently, the board doesn’t appraise property but sometimes auditors “examine asset values reported by taxpayers to ensure accuracy,” he said.
Chris Parker, a former attorney for the tax board who now works as a tax attorney with the firm Baker Tilly, said the board has “no way of knowing anyone’s net wealth.”

Ariel Jurow Kleiman, a tax policy professor at the University of Southern California, doesn’t think the state would have a hard time putting the tax into effect. Stocks, which make up a substantial part of billionaires’ wealth, are easily valued, she said. For more “bespoke” property like art and jewelry, California could look to the Internal Revenue Service’s federal tax on inherited property.
“There are commonsense methods like looking at comparable assets or looking to available markets to see how comps are valued,” she said. “We wouldn’t be asking people to reinvent the wheel here.”
Experts do expect disputes over the value of privately held businesses.
